insight.title: The Largest Waterfall on Earth Is Underwater
insight.subtitle: Hidden beneath the North Atlantic is a cascading ocean current three times taller than any waterfall on land.

sections.text: Deep beneath the surface between Greenland and Iceland lies the Denmark Strait cataract. Here, cold polar water plunges over two miles down a massive submarine cliff into the ocean’s abyssal depth.

The colossal drop is driven entirely by temperature. Because freezing Arctic water is denser than the warmer ocean surrounding it, it sinks rapidly, cascading like a subterranean river across the seafloor.

This single underwater waterfall carries three million cubic meters of water per second—carrying over fifty thousand times more water than Niagara Falls, operating in total silence and absolute darkness.
Earth’s grandest waterfall flows unseen beneath the waves.

audioBrief.script:
Welcome to your Sift Daily Briefing. Here is the clear, plain version of today's news.

Iran is negotiating rocket launcher sales and a new treaty with Russia. The report of the deal emerged from recent diplomatic discussions. Top Iranian security official Mohsen Rezaei met with Russian President Vladimir Putin. Rezaei and Putin discussed developing a cooperation treaty between their nations. It remains unannounced when the rocket launcher sales will officially take place.

Next, the United States added 165,000 jobs to the economy in October. The Bureau of Labor Statistics reported that the unemployment rate fell slightly to 4.1 percent. Average hourly earnings increased at an annual rate of 3.1 percent. Earlier job figures for August and September were revised up by 84,000 jobs. Outplacement firm Challenger, Gray and Christmas tracked under 44,000 layoffs in October. That was a 71 percent decrease compared with last October. Gas prices are on average one dollar a gallon higher than last year. The Federal Reserve kept interest rates steady in October between 3.75 percent and 4 percent. Economists expect the central bank to hike interest rates again in December.

Turning to technology, stock futures for the tech-heavy Nasdaq index rose on Friday. A recent market decline had wiped nearly three trillion dollars off the S&P 500 index. Investors feared that Democratic control of Congress could bring tougher rules for artificial intelligence. Nvidia, the company that makes most AI chips, rose 4.5 percent in pre-market trading. Other chip companies like AMD and Intel gained between 4.6 percent and 8.2 percent. Electric car maker Tesla rose two percent, while rocket builder SpaceX gained four percent. The CBOE Volatility Index, which measures Wall Street fear, dropped slightly to 26.70. Traders now see over a 65 percent chance of an interest rate hike in December.

In legal news, Meta, Google, and TikTok sued California Attorney General Rob Bonta. The tech companies want to block a new state law called Assembly Bill 1709. Governor Gavin Newsom signed the bill into law back in September. The law prohibits platforms from offering autoplay videos to users under 16 years old. It also stops companies from using personalized content feeds for those young users. Violators face fines of up to 50,000 dollars per affected user under 16. Meta argues that the law violates free speech rights under the First Amendment. A spokesperson for YouTube owner Google said autoplay is already off by default for minors. California's attorney general office said it will defend the law in court.

Moving to politics, voters across several states passed ballot measures on social issues. Voters in Arizona, Colorado, and Washington approved restrictions on transgender youth in school sports. Colorado was also on track to ban gender-affirming surgery for minors. An NCAA representative confirmed that zero transgender athletes currently compete in women's college leagues. Four states voted on abortion measures, and all four preserved their existing legal status. In Missouri, nearly 56 percent of voters rejected a proposed ban on abortion. Nevada and Virginia voted to protect abortion rights in their state constitutions. Idaho voters chose to maintain the state's existing total ban on abortion. In Massachusetts, nearly 76 percent of voters chose to keep recreational marijuana legal.

Finally, United States election results could affect future government funding for Ukraine. Democratic congressional aides told Reuters that sending aid to Ukraine will be a top priority. Democrats won majorities in both the Senate and the House of Representatives. They may hold 56 Senate seats and nearly 260 seats in the House. President Donald Trump has previously slowed or blocked aid passed by Congress. Trump recently signed a deal to import Russian diesel and waived some Russian sanctions. A White House official stated that Trump remains committed to ending the war. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said he hopes the election brings more support. Lawmakers can override presidential vetoes if they build two-thirds majorities in Congress.

Up next, Mark Carney unveils a budget to strengthen Canada's economy as Trump's trade war continues.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney unveiled a new national budget on Thursday. The plan aims to make Canada less dependent on the United States. It proposes over 101 billion U.S. dollars in multiyear spending and tax breaks. The government expects economic growth of just one percent in 2026. A tax break for business investments will cost almost 26 billion U.S. dollars over five years. Carney wants to double Canadian exports outside the United States by 2035. The budget includes nearly 18 billion U.S. dollars for a new national wealth fund. Canada stopped trade talks in August after Carney said U.S. demands threatened Canadian sovereignty.

Next, the United States Senate is preparing to vote on a new energy infrastructure bill. The bill is called the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act. Two Democratic and two Republican senators sponsored the 417-page proposal. It creates deadlines to speed up the approval process for energy projects. The White House supports the bill to cut review times. The American Clean Power Association says it could unlock 350 gigawatts of clean energy. Think tank Rhodium Group says a best-case result cuts household energy bills by 78 dollars. However, researcher Kevin Kircher found the bill could actually increase overall energy sector emissions. The Senate is scheduled to vote on the measure on November ninth.

Turning to climate news, a new United Nations report says millions of refugees face extreme weather hazards. Nearly 90 million refugees live in places exposed to severe droughts, floods, and heat. Countries hosting large refugee populations receive only ten percent of global climate funding. Refugee Monira Bahraldin fled Sudan in 2023 and now faces severe heat and drought in Chad. The report says one in three sub-Saharan refugee settlements will face extreme heat by 2050. Floods are expected to force three million people in eastern Africa from their homes this year. Most refugees who returned home in early 2026 went back to climate-vulnerable countries.

In space technology news, company Blue Origin delayed its next rocket launch from December to January. The delay follows an explosion at their launch pad nearly six months ago. Startup Argo Space is building satellites that run on water instead of standard fuel. Their spacecraft split liquid water into hydrogen and oxygen to produce thrust. In Japan, Interstellar Technologies received up to 76 million dollars from the national space agency. The company plans to launch its Zero rocket carrying one metric ton by 2027. Research firm Quilty Space reports the world faces a shortage of 150 launches by 2030.

Switching to business news, jewelry sales in Hong Kong reached 5.8 billion U.S. dollars this year. Sales jumped 22 percent during the first nine months compared to the previous year. Wealthy Chinese buyers are purchasing gold and gemstones to preserve their wealth. China’s government recently increased tax inspections on foreign investments owned by its citizens. While mainland luxury sales fell over ten percent, Hong Kong jewelry stores saw strong demand. Insurance agent Manna Wang said her mainland clients now ask to shop for physical gold. Total visitor numbers to Hong Kong increased by 12 percent over the first nine months.

Finally, France is paying record interest rates to borrow money as its public debt grows. French national debt has reached around 120 percent of its gross domestic product. France now pays nearly 1.6 percentage points more interest on bonds than Germany. The borrowing gap between the two countries doubled after June 2026. To address protests, France promised four billion euros for schools and one billion for universities. Statistic agency INSEE reports 56 percent of French residents receive more government benefits than they pay. France is expected to pay over 79 billion euros in interest costs during 2026.

Before we go, here is your thought for the day.

Deep between Greenland and Iceland lies the world's largest waterfall, located entirely underwater. It is called the Denmark Strait cataract. Freezing Arctic water plunges over two miles down an ocean cliff. Because freezing water is cold and dense, it sinks beneath the warmer surrounding water. This massive underwater river flows silently in total darkness. It moves three million cubic meters of water every single second. That is over fifty thousand times more water than Niagara Falls. Nature creates incredible wonders in places we cannot easily see. What other hidden forces might be shaping our ocean depths without us knowing?

Thank you for spending a few minutes listening to the Sift Daily Briefing.

audioBriefIndepth.script:
Welcome to your Sift In-Depth Briefing. This is our full analysis of the big stories shaping your world today.

Iran is currently negotiating rocket launcher sales and a new treaty with Russia. This report comes as top Iranian security official Mohsen Rezaei discusses developing a cooperation treaty with Vladimir Putin. Iran and Russia are working to deepen their political and military relations through these negotiation talks.

Now, let us turn to the American economy and the latest job market numbers.

Did the United States economy create more jobs than expected in October? American employers added 165,000 jobs, surpassing expectations from top financial economists.

Let us look at how the American job market reached this point. After pandemic lockdowns ended, the nation experienced a strong hiring boom. In 2021 and 2022, monthly job creation averaged 491,000 jobs. Later, high interest rates and trade policies reduced hiring across the country. In 2025, monthly job creation dropped to an average of just 9,700 jobs. Employers kept their current workers but were slow to hire new ones. Economists called this situation a low-fire and low-hire environment. At the same time, inflation remained high for several years. Prices for food and essentials grew faster than worker wages. A war with Iran also pushed up energy costs. Gasoline prices rose above four dollars a gallon on average. That is about one dollar a gallon higher than a year ago. Diesel fuel costs are 60 percent higher compared with prewar levels. Diesel powers large transport vehicles throughout the national supply chain. These rising expenses left many Americans feeling squeezed financially.

What changed was the outcome of the recent midterm elections. Voters handed full control of the United States Congress to Democrats. Multiple polls showed voters were frustrated about higher gas and grocery prices. Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union, noted the economy is squeezing people financially.

That brings us to today's news from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. The United States added 165,000 jobs in October. The unemployment rate dipped slightly to 4.1 percent. Figures for August and September were revised up by 84,000 jobs total. Healthcare, transportation, warehousing, and manufacturing added jobs. Layoffs in September fell to their lowest level in eighteen months. Outplacement firm Challenger, Gray and Christmas tracked under 44,000 layoffs in October. That was a 71 percent decrease compared with last October. Gross domestic product advanced at a 3.4 percent annual pace from July through September. Average hourly earnings increased at an annual rate of 3.1 percent. However, wage growth remained lower than September's annualized inflation rate of 3.7 percent.

Why is this job growth happening at this moment? Employers want to retain existing workers because replacing them is difficult. Fewer people are entering the labor pool due to retirements and immigration crackdowns. Yale University's Budget Lab estimates the break-even point is now just over 5,000 jobs monthly.

What does this mean for you, and what should we watch next? This report shows the labor market remains resilient despite economic shocks. In September, the Federal Reserve raised interest rates to between 3.75 and 4 percent. Officials then kept rates steady at their October meeting held before the election. Economists expect the central bank to consider another interest rate hike in December. Higher rates can curb inflation, but they also increase borrowing costs for families.

Next, let us examine why technology stocks fell sharply before making a partial recovery.

Why did major technology stocks fall sharply before making a partial recovery? Stocks rebounded after fears about data center rules and artificial intelligence spending caused a steep sell-off.

Let us trace how financial markets arrived at this moment. Over recent years, artificial intelligence pushed stock markets to record highs in 2026. Technology companies spent vast amounts of money building energy-intensive data centers. These large tech firms leading the build-out are called hyperscalers. However, local communities raised concerns about the environmental impact of these data centers. At the same time, investors questioned if AI revenues would justify the high spending. A jump in crude oil prices also raised worries about inflation and higher interest rates.

What changed was the recent midterm election result. Democrats won elections in key data center states. Political research firm Redbud Consulting reported voters approved over 40 local ballot measures restricting data centers. Investors worried these victories would lead to tighter rules and slower spending on data centers. On Thursday, a sell-off wiped nearly three trillion dollars off the market value of S&P 500 companies. The Nasdaq Composite logged its steepest one-day fall in 19 months. This fall pushed the index into correction territory, meaning a drop of 10 percent from its peak.

That brings us to today's news from Wall Street. On Friday morning, stock futures and key technology shares began to stabilize. The Nasdaq Composite rose 437 points, or 1.8 percent, in early trading. The S&P 500 climbed 72 points, or nearly one percent. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 129 points, or 0.2 percent. Chipmaker Nvidia gained 6.6 percent after its worst day since January 2025. Micron Technology rose 9.8 percent, while Alphabet gained 2 percent and Meta rose 2.4 percent. Other chip stocks like AMD, Intel, Broadcom, and Micron rose between 4.6 and 8.2 percent. Data center operators IREN and Applied Digital recovered from heavy losses in the previous session. Elon Musk-led Tesla rose 2 percent, while SpaceX gained 4 percent. Wall Street's fear gauge, the CBOE Volatility Index, dropped slightly on Friday to 26.70. Software firm Atlassian dropped 14.1 percent after reporting its first-quarter results.

Why are investors reacting in this way right now? Financial markets collided with concerns about policy changes, AI spending, and inflation all at once. Jane Gibbons, an equity strategist at Jefferies, called Thursday's sell-off a reactionary move rather than a fundamental reset.

What does this mean for you, and what should we watch next? The partial rebound shows tech stocks have not lost all investor confidence. However, analysts are watching whether AI companies can deliver real revenue growth. Vicky Redwood, economic adviser at Capital Economics, expects AI capital expenditures to slow next year. She notes this slowdown could drag on overall economic growth in the United States. Watch the upcoming public market debut of AI firm Anthropic on the Nasdaq this month. Its performance will show if investors remain willing to fund growing AI firms.

Up next, Meta, Google, and TikTok sue California AG over teen social media law.

Can California stop social media apps from showing automatic videos to kids? Major tech companies are suing the state to block a new law.

For years, platforms like Instagram, YouTube, and TikTok used smart computer programs. These programs pick videos based on what users like to watch. They also play videos automatically one after another without stopping. State leaders around the world became worried about these features. They argued that automatic videos make teenagers spend too much time online. They claimed this focus on app feeds harms teen mental health. In December twenty twenty-five, Australia became the first country to ban social media for kids under sixteen. France tried to pass a similar law, but its top court struck it down over free speech concerns. Tech companies also faced legal pressure over child safety. Meta agreed to pay a settlement of up to eighteen billion dollars to clear state claims.

In September, California Governor Gavin Newsom signed a new bill called AB 1709. This law stops platforms from giving users under sixteen personalized feeds or automatic videos. It also orders apps to delete teen accounts if those features are not turned off.

Now, Meta, Google, and TikTok have filed separate lawsuits against California Attorney General Rob Bonta. Meta argues the law violates the First Amendment, which protects free expression online. Meta says it would have to change its speech rules or delete minor accounts completely. A TikTok spokesperson said the law restricts free expression just like curating books or television. Google said YouTube already turns off autoplay for minors by default. If companies disobey, they could pay fines up to fifty thousand dollars per child. A representative for Attorney General Bonta said his office will defend California's commonsense rules.

Companies are rushing to court now because the law takes effect at the start of the new year. They want a judge to halt the rules before enforcement begins.

Digital safety experts like Rindala Alajaji warn the law could actually harm online privacy. She says apps may require age checks, which collects more personal data from everyone. She also notes social media lets teens organize important political movements. Courts could block the law, or California might force social media apps to change worldwide.

Now, let us turn to recent election results across the United States.

Did a major Democratic election victory mean voters agreed on every social issue? State election results showed that voters hold very different views on abortion, drugs, and transgender rights.

In American elections, citizens choose leaders, but they also vote on specific state rules. These direct votes on public policies are called ballot measures. Four years ago, the Supreme Court overruled Roe v. Wade, ending nationwide federal abortion rights. Since then, twenty-six states have added legal protections for abortion access. Meanwhile, national debates grew over medical care and school sports for transgender youth. Existing data suggests about three hundred thousand American teenagers identify as transgender. Medical data shows surgical care for minors is rare or virtually nonexistent. An athletic group confirmed zero transgender athletes currently compete in women's college sports. Over the last two years, the Trump administration targeted youth gender care and pushed strict drug laws.

In recent elections, Democrats won control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate. However, voters in different states still passed very different ballot measures.

Voters in Arizona, Colorado, and Washington approved restrictions on transgender youth in school sports. Colorado also voted to ban gender-affirming surgery for minors and raise penalties for selling fentanyl. On abortion, four states voted and kept their current legal rules. Nearly fifty-six percent of Missouri voters rejected a proposed constitutional abortion ban. Nevada and Virginia protected abortion rights, while Idaho kept its abortion ban. Massachusetts voters chose to keep recreational marijuana legal, with nearly seventy-six percent voting to keep it. California voters supported Proposition 38, approving eight point four billion dollars for immunology research. Half of that funding, four point two billion dollars, goes to one institute cofounded by Gary Michelson. Michelson spent over forty million dollars of his own money supporting the measure.

These ballot results made headlines because they happened alongside the major national election. Voters wanted to set state laws on health care, crime, and scientific research funding.

ACLU leader Chase Strangio said spending heavily influences these ballot measure outcomes. In Colorado, state lawmakers could still amend the statutory changes before enforcing them. Colorado's governor-elect said the state must take a long, hard look at the restrictions first. Observers will watch how state leaders adjust these laws in the coming months.

Next, we look across the ocean at the ongoing war in Ukraine.

Will recent Democratic election victories in Congress lead to more military aid for Ukraine? Democratic leaders plan to push for new support, but President Donald Trump could block their efforts.

Russia invaded Ukraine in twenty twenty-two, beginning a long and difficult war. The United States sent billions of dollars in weapons to help Ukraine defend its land. In January twenty twenty-five, Donald Trump began his second presidential term. His Republican party took control of both chambers of Congress. Since then, Congress has not passed any major new aid legislation for Ukraine. The Trump administration also slowed down aid approved before he took office. Trump frequently uses executive authority to run foreign policy without asking Congress first. He recently waived sanctions against Russia and signed a deal to import Russian diesel fuel. Meanwhile, Russian forces keep launching heavy attacks on Ukrainian cities and energy networks.

Recently, Democrats won sweeping election victories to take back the House and Senate. This election outcome gives opposition lawmakers new power over federal spending and oversight.

Democratic aides say increasing help for Ukraine will be a top priority starting in January. Democratic Senator Dick Durbin said Congress must find ways to make the administration follow the law. A White House official stated Trump wants the war settled so senseless killing ends. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said he hopes Democratic gains will yield more military aid. Democrats may control fifty-six Senate seats and nearly two hundred sixty House seats. With some Republican support, Democrats could reach the two-thirds majority needed to override presidential vetoes. Leaders could also attach Ukraine aid to must-pass national defense budget bills. Aides said Democrats already sent letters to companies to preserve records for possible Russian business investigations.

This battle is starting now because the new Congress takes office in January. Also, three-way peace talks between the United States, Russia, and Ukraine resume next week.

Analyst Orysia Lutsevych says a Democratic Congress could limit Trump's plans for closer ties with Russia. Strategic adviser Price Floyd warns Trump may simply ignore whatever Congress decides to pass. Expert Charles Lichfield notes Ukraine faces a brutal winter with damaged power infrastructure. Observers will watch whether bipartisan votes can force new Ukraine assistance past the White House.

Up next, Mark Carney unveils a budget to boost Canada's economy during Trump's trade war.

How can Canada protect its economy during a trade war with the United States? Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney unveiled a budget aimed at making Canada less dependent on America. Canada and the United States share a very long border and a close economic relationship. For many years, the two countries traded goods easily back and forth with each other. Canadian companies sold most of their products directly to buyers in the United States. Then, Donald Trump became the president of the United States. President Trump started a trade war by placing taxes on goods coming into America. This trade war created big problems for Canadian businesses that rely on American shoppers. Canada tried to negotiate a new trade agreement with the United States. However, Canada walked away from those trade talks in August. Mark Carney said American demands threatened Canadian culture and Canadian sovereignty. Canada decided it needed a fresh plan to build its own economic strength. So, the Canadian government unveiled a sweeping economic budget on Thursday. The budget plan is titled Masters of Our Destiny. It proposes 142.1 billion Canadian dollars, or 101.6 billion U.S. dollars, in spending and tax breaks. Total Canadian spending is projected at 603 billion Canadian dollars, or 431 billion U.S. dollars. The government projects a deficit of 62.3 billion Canadian dollars for 2026 and 2027. That is 3 billion Canadian dollars less than forecast in April. Canada's combined government deficits equal 2.5 percent of its economy. In contrast, the U.S. deficit equals 8.5 percent of its economy. The budget explicitly declares that the United States is upending global trade. Because of trade troubles, Canada forecasts economic growth of just 1 percent in 2026. Growth is expected to reach 1.7 percent in 2027. A tax break costing 36 billion Canadian dollars will cut effective business tax rates to 6.4 percent. This budget arrived two days after the U.S. midterm elections. Democrats swept those elections, which weakened Donald Trump's political position. Canada wants to act while the two countries pursue a possible trade agreement. Canada wants to double its exports outside the United States by 2035. Mark Carney aims to forge closer ties with nations in Europe and Asia. Canada is creating a 25 billion Canadian dollar sovereign wealth fund to support local companies. It also outlines 7.7 billion Canadian dollars to strengthen its defense industry. Canada says it is on track to meet NATO defense goals by 2035. However, the budget does not fully account for the total defense cost.

That shift in Canada brings us to another major policy debate inside the United States. How could a new bill change the way America builds power lines and energy plants? A group of senators proposed a law to cut red tape for energy projects. Building large energy projects in the United States requires permission from federal agencies. Companies must get federal permits before constructing power plants, transmission lines, or pipelines. Old environmental laws like the Clean Water Act protect public lands from industrial pollution. However, getting these permits has become very slow and complicated over time. Large energy projects can spend many years waiting for final official approvals. Many leaders argue that slow approvals prevent new energy from reaching the power grid quickly. Solar and wind power are currently among the cheapest sources of electricity available. Supporters believe faster approvals will help cheap clean power expand faster than fossil fuels. Meanwhile, computer data centers are putting heavy new demand on the electrical grid. This rising power demand has prompted companies to plan many new natural gas plants. Four senators introduced a sweeping 417-page bill to speed up environmental reviews. Now, the Senate is set to vote on this plan on November 9. The proposal is called the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act. Two Republicans and two Democrats sponsored the bill, and the White House backs it. The American Clean Power Association says it could unlock 350 gigawatts of clean energy. Research by the Rhodium Group found the bill could cut overall emissions by 4 percent. That study says it could also save households 78 U.S. dollars each year. Another report from Resources for the Future says it could cut power emissions 6 percent by 2041. However, the Natural Resources Defense Council warns that shorter reviews could harm public lands. Energy modeler Kevin Kircher found that emissions could actually rise above baseline levels. He warned that health risks from air pollution would also increase. Lawmakers want to vote on this bill before the next Congress takes office. Democrats won recent midterm elections and will soon control both chambers of Congress. However, any future law will still require a signature from President Trump. If passed, this law could speed up construction for clean energy and fossil fuels alike. Lower energy prices might encourage people to use more power overall. That increased demand could push emissions higher if natural gas expands rapidly. Observers are watching how senators vote on this measure on November 9.

While Washington debates energy rules, millions of refugees face dangerous weather around the world. Why are refugees suffering the worst effects of global climate change right now? A new report shows that most refugees live in countries facing severe climate dangers. Violent conflict forces millions of vulnerable families to flee their homes every single year. These displaced people often move into temporary shelters in fragile neighboring countries. At the same time, global temperatures are causing worse droughts, heatwaves, and severe floods. Refugees did not cause climate change, but they live on the front lines of it. Severe weather destroys temporary shelters and undermines the way displaced families earn a living. Many host countries lack the money needed to build protection against harsh climate events. Stateless people face extra challenges because they lack official legal recognition. Without legal recognition, stateless families struggle to access relief after natural disasters strike. The United Nations refugee agency published a new report called No Escape III on Friday. The UN report states that three in four refugees live in high-hazard climate zones. That figure equals nearly 90 million vulnerable people across the globe. Yet, fragile host countries receive only about 10 percent of global climate funding. Assistant High Commissioner Antón Leis García said refugees face a double injustice. Monira Bahraldin fled war in Darfur, Sudan, to live in a camp in Chad. She explained that severe heat makes long trips to fetch water even harder for families. Heavy El Niño flooding is expected to displace 3 million people across East Africa this year. In Syria, nearly 4 million people returned home, but May floods damaged houses along the river. This UN report was published right before the COP31 climate conference opens next week in Türkiye. UN officials want world leaders to direct concrete investments to high-risk communities. By 2050, one in three refugee camps in sub-Saharan Africa could face 100 hot days yearly. Local refugees are testing solutions like solar water pumps and planting protective mangrove trees. Observers will watch whether leaders at COP31 direct more funding to displaced communities.

Next, the Rocket Report looks at Artemis II tearing through the atmosphere and new delays for New Glenn.

Why are rocket companies struggling to keep up with space launches right now? A new report shows the world faces a shortage of rocket launches over the next five years.

Space companies build rockets to lift satellites into orbit around Earth. For many years, a few big companies and government agencies controlled most space launches. Then private companies started building cheaper rockets. SpaceX changed the industry by making rockets that can land and fly again. But building rockets is hard and full of long delays. Rocket engines can break during ground tests or early flights. War in Ukraine also took Russian rockets off the Western market. Meanwhile, companies like Amazon want to launch thousands of internet satellites. That means launch demand has grown much faster than the number of working rockets.

Analytics firm Quilty Space released a new report looking at global rocket supply. Quilty Space estimates a shortfall of about 150 launches between now and 2030 compared to satellite demand. That launch shortage could double if the United States military needs more launches. That happens if SpaceX does not extend its Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy program to meet those needs. Caleb Henry at Quilty Space says the launch crisis will not go away this decade for sure. 

Blue Origin announced a minor delay for its New Glenn rocket return to flight from December until January. Blue Origin is still rebuilding its launch pad after an explosion nearly six months ago. There is pent-up demand from NASA, Amazon, and the Space Force for New Glenn to fly. Blue Origin also revealed a new kick stage and a new engine design. 

Three brothers who worked at SpaceX founded Argo Space in late 2022 to build satellites using water. Argo Space satellites will use water as a propellant, coolant, and radiation shield. Its first mission in July failed after a solar array failed to deploy properly. Two more test missions are scheduled for 2027.

In Japan, launcher startup Interstellar Technologies secured backing from space agency JAXA for its Zero rocket. The government-funded program offers grants of up to 76 million dollars per company. Interstellar previously raised more than 250 million dollars. Its Zero rocket carries up to one metric ton, or 2,200 pounds, to low Earth orbit. Interstellar achieved Japan's first successful test firing of an orbital class methane engine. Its president Satoshi Nakayama says they must turn test results into commercial services quickly. Interstellar targets a first launch of Zero in 2027.

China also launched 18 more satellites for its SpaceSail internet network using a Kinetica 2 rocket. Developer CAS Space built Kinetica 2 with three side-by-side boosters like SpaceX's Falcon Heavy. The SpaceSail network now consists of about 275 flat-panel satellites out of a planned 1,296.

India launched its NVS 03 navigation satellite on October 30 using a GSLV rocket. The satellite carries multiple atomic clocks of different designs after older satellites suffered clock failures. Indian officials nicknamed the rocket naughty boy because six of its 20 launches failed in the past.

Rocket delays are piling up just as satellite operators need more launches than ever. Satellite internet services and science missions could face delays over the coming years. Quilty Space research suggests the launch shortage might not abate until late in the 2030s. Watch to see if new rockets like New Glenn and Zero meet their target launch dates.

Moving from space down to retail markets, another big shift is happening in Asia.

Why are wealthy Chinese buyers rushing to buy gold jewellery in Hong Kong right now? Hong Kong jewellery sales surged 22 percent as mainland buyers sought safe ways to store their money.

For many years, wealthy people in mainland China grew their money by buying real estate. Others put money into foreign stocks, offshore accounts, or insurance policies. But China experienced a prolonged property downturn that trapped household savings. An artificial intelligence stock market rally also soured recently. At the same time, authorities in Beijing tightened scrutiny on overseas assets. Officials restricted mainland firms from listing stock in Hong Kong. They also increased checks on foreign trusts and offshore stock trading. Because of these rules, rich buyers wanted safer places to store their wealth. They wanted items less vulnerable to tax changes and regulatory shifts.

Chinese tax authorities stepped up their scrutiny of wealthy citizens' overseas assets and investments. Government data shows Hong Kong jewellery and watch sales jumped 22 percent. Sales reached 45.8 billion Hong Kong dollars, or about 5.8 billion United States dollars, in nine months. This sector accounted for about 15 percent of Hong Kong's total retail sales. Mainland luxury spending fell over 10 percent, but Hong Kong jewellery sales kept growing. 

Insurance agent Manna Wang said her clients spent up to 15,000 dollars per person buying gold. Hong Kong prices can be more than five percent lower than the mainland because Hong Kong is tax-free. A strong yuan also makes exchange rates more favorable for mainland tourists. 

Jewellery sales at company LVMH grew eight percent, while Kering jewellery sales jumped 17 percent. Meanwhile, Kering fashion and leather goods sales fell two percent. Shares of jeweller Laopu rose more than eight percent after gold prices rallied. Luk Fook stock also gained five percent. Visitor arrivals to Hong Kong rose 12 percent, reaching 87 percent of 2018 levels. Global brands like Audemars Piguet, FOPE, Tiffany and Van Cleef are opening or expanding boutiques in Hong Kong. Alexis Bonhomme of Trinity Asia said gold jewellery offers reassurance and lasting value to traveling clients.

Mainland buyers are prioritising keeping their money safe right now instead of looking for big growth. Global luxury brands may rely more on Hong Kong to protect their overall sales. Watch to see if Chinese authorities add tighter rules on physical gold purchases in the future.

From shopping streets in Hong Kong, we now turn to government budgets in Europe.

Why are investors getting worried about the money the French government owes to lenders? France must pay much higher interest rates on its borrowing after a surge in market risk premiums.

Governments borrow money by issuing bonds to investors. Investors buy these bonds and earn interest over time. If a country pays back its debts reliably, investors ask for lower interest rates. Germany carries a highest possible AAA credit rating and pays lower interest rates. France has spent more than it collects in tax revenue every year since 1974. Over time, that continuous spending built up a very large pile of national debt. 

Meanwhile, political parties in France split into competing groups with very different ideas. The French government currently lacks a single majority in parliament to pass budget cuts. Statistics agency INSEE says 56 percent of people get more in government benefits than they pay in taxes. Protests across France pushed the government to promise billions of euros in new spending for schools and universities. The government plans to provide four billion euros in low-interest loans for school renovations by 2030. It also promised one billion euros for universities by 2029.

France's public debt stands at around 120 percent of its gross domestic product. Germany carries a debt ratio of roughly 65 percent despite its own large investment package. France pays nearly 1.6 percentage points more interest than Germany on 10-year bonds. The interest gap between France and Germany has more than doubled since June 2026. 

France expects to pay over 79 billion euros in debt interest in 2026. That interest bill is projected to reach between 125 billion and 132 billion euros by 2030. Agence France Tresor estimates the central government interest bill alone is 62.6 billion euros. RN leader Marine Le Pen promises 140 billion euros in savings while lowering the retirement age to 62. LFI leader Jean-Luc Melenchon suggested central bank bonds could be thrown into the fire. Economist Friedrich Heinemann called promises from political extremes fairy tales that ignore real financial limits. Researcher Landry Charrier noted that euro usage hid these spending pressures for a long time.

France must soon replace older bonds that carried low interest rates with new, much more expensive debt. Higher interest bills mean France will have less money for public services in the coming years. If interest costs keep rising, French banks could face stress that hurts the broader European economy. Watch whether French lawmakers can agree on budget cuts before borrowing costs rise even further.

Now, let us step away from world news for a moment.

Before we go, here is your thought for the day.

Deep beneath the ocean surface between Greenland and Iceland lies the largest waterfall on Earth. It is called the Denmark Strait cataract. Here, cold polar water plunges over two miles down a massive submarine cliff into the ocean depth. 

This colossal drop is driven entirely by temperature. Freezing Arctic water is denser than the warmer ocean water surrounding it. Because it is heavier, the cold water sinks rapidly toward the sea floor. It cascades like a giant subterranean river across the ocean bottom. 

This single underwater waterfall carries three million cubic meters of water per second. That is over fifty thousand times more water than Niagara Falls. Yet it operates in total silence and absolute darkness. Earth's grandest waterfall flows completely unseen beneath the waves. How many other magnificent processes happen every day without anyone ever watching them?

Thank you for listening to Sift In-Depth today. We hope you take a peaceful moment to ponder the quiet wonders around us.
